question.text:
Let $F(x) = x^2$ for $x\in\mathbb R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ to $x\in \mathbb R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

\[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n \cos(nx) + b_n \sin(nx)\right). \] Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient $a_5$ below, where $\langle \:,\rangle$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[-\pi,\pi).$
question.explanation:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ is given by \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that's piecewise continuous over $x\in [-\pi,\pi),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left( a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \] where $a_0,$ $a_n,$ and $b_n$ are constants to be determined.

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\cos(5x){:}$

\begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \cos(5x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \cos(5x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2},\cos(5x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle a_n\cos(nx), \cos(5x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle b_n\sin(nx), \cos(5x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1,\cos(5x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \left\langle \cos(nx), \cos(5x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n \left\langle \sin(nx), \cos(5x) \right\rangle \end{align*}

Since the functions $ 1, \sin(x), \cos(x), \sin(2x), \cos(2x), \ldots $ are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is \[ a_5 \left\langle \cos(5x), \cos(5x) \right\rangle. \] Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle \cos(5x), \cos(5x) \right\rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \cos^2(5x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(10x) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} x + \dfrac{1}{20} \sin(10x) \right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} (\pi - (-\pi)) - \dfrac{1}{20} (\sin(10\pi) - (\sin(-10\pi))) \\[5pt] &= \pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain that \begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \cos(5x) \right\rangle &= a_5 \left\langle \cos(5x), \cos(5x) \right\rangle \\[5pt] a_5 &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{\left\langle f(x), \cos(5x) \right\rangle}{\left\langle \cos(5x), \cos(5x) \right\rangle} }\\[5pt] a_5 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x)\cos(5x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{\pi} } \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} x^2\cos(5x)\,\textrm{d}x}. \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{-\pi}^{\pi} f(x) g(x) \, \textrm{d}x \]

Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [-\pi,\pi)$ defined above, select the correct options below.
question.explanation:
We begin by using the product-to-sum identity \[ \sin(4x)\sin(7x) =\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\cos(3x)-\cos(11x)\big). \]

Substituting this into the integral gives \begin{align*} \langle \sin(4x), \sin(7x) \rangle &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \sin(4x)\sin(7x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}\cos(3x)-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(11x)\:\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{6} \sin(3x)-\dfrac{1}{22}\sin(11x)\right]_{-\pi}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6}\big(\sin(3\pi)-\sin(-3\pi)\big) -\dfrac{1}{22}\big(\sin(11\pi)-\sin(-11\pi)\big) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{6}(0-0)-\dfrac{1}{22}(0-0) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $f(x)=\sin(4x)$ and $g(x)=\sin(7x)$ $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{are orthogonal}}$ with respect to the inner product.

example.title: Checking Orthogonality of Sines and Cosines

question.text:
Let $F(x) = 3x-4$ for $x\in\mathbb R,$ and let $f(x)$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of $F$ from $x\in [0,2\pi)$ to $x\in \mathbb R.$ The Fourier series of $f$ is given by

\[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left(a_n \cos(nx) + b_n \sin(nx)\right). \] Select the correct options in the expression for the coefficient $a_7$ below, where $\langle \:,\rangle$ denotes the usual inner product on functions over $[0,2\pi).$
question.explanation:
The usual inner product of functions $f$ and $g$ over $x\in [0,2\pi)$ is given by \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x)g(x)\,\textrm{d}x. \]

For a $2\pi$-periodic function $f(x)$ that is piecewise continuous over $x\in [0,2\pi),$ the Fourier series of $f$ is given by \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left( a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \] where $a_0,$ $a_n,$ and $b_n$ are constants to be determined.

Now, we find the inner product of $f(x)$ with $\cos(7x){:}$

\begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \cos(7x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\right), \cos(7x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \left\langle \dfrac{a_0}{2},\cos(7x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle a_n\cos(nx), \cos(7x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \left\langle b_n\sin(nx), \cos(7x) \right\rangle &=\\[5pt] \dfrac{a_0}{2} \left\langle 1,\cos(7x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n \left\langle \cos(nx), \cos(7x) \right\rangle + \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}b_n \left\langle \sin(nx), \cos(7x) \right\rangle \end{align*}

Since the functions $ 1, \sin(x), \cos(x), \sin(2x), \cos(2x), \ldots $ are orthogonal with respect to the defined inner product, the only nonzero term in the final expression above is \[ a_7 \left\langle \cos(7x), \cos(7x) \right\rangle. \]

Computing the inner product, we have \begin{align*} \left\langle \cos(7x), \cos(7x) \right\rangle &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \cos^2(7x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(14x) \:\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ \dfrac{1}{2} x + \dfrac{1}{28} \sin(14x) \right]_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{2} (2\pi - 0) - \dfrac{1}{28} (\sin(28\pi) - \sin(0)) \\[5pt] &= \pi. \end{align*}

Finally, we obtain that \begin{align*} \left\langle f(x), \cos(7x) \right\rangle &= a_7 \left\langle \cos(7x), \cos(7x) \right\rangle \\[5pt] a_7 &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{\left\langle f(x), \cos(7x) \right\rangle}{\left\langle \cos(7x), \cos(7x) \right\rangle} }\\[5pt] a_7 &= \dfrac{1}{\pi} \int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x)\cos(7x)\,\textrm{d}x \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{1}{\pi} } \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\int_{0}^{2\pi} (3x-4)\cos(7x)\,\textrm{d}x}. \end{align*}

question.text:
Let $F(x) = \cos(3x)$ for $x\in\mathbb R.$ Suppose $f(x)$ is the $\dfrac{\pi}3$-periodic extension of $F(x)$ from $x \in \left[0,\dfrac{\pi}3\right)$ to $x \in \mathbb{R}.$ Which of the following statements are true?

  1. $f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}3\right) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  2. $f(x) = F(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
  3. $f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = f(x)$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$
question.explanation:
Since $f$ is the $\dfrac{\pi}3$-periodic extension of $F,$ we have

  • $f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}3\right)=f(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb{R},$ and

  • $f(x)=F(x)$ for all $x\in\left[0\dfrac{\pi}3\right).$

With that in mind, we examine each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is true. This is exactly the definition of $\pi/3$-periodicity: \[ f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}3\right) =f(x) \] for all $x\in\mathbb{R}.$

  • Statement II is false. For example, take $x=\dfrac{\pi}3.$ Then, \begin{align*} f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = f\left(0+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = f\left(0\right) = F\left(0\right) = \cos\left(0\right) = 1, \end{align*} while \begin{align*} F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\left(3 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos(\pi) = -1. \end{align*} Hence, $f(x) \neq F(x)$ for $x=\dfrac{\pi}3.$

  • Statement III is false. For example, take $x=0.$ Then, \begin{align*} f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = f\left(0+ \dfrac{\pi}{6} \right) = f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6} \right)= F\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6} \right) =\cos\left(3 \cdot \dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) = 0, \end{align*} while \begin{align*} f(x) = f(0) = 1. \end{align*} Hence, $f\left(x+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \neq f(x)$ for $x = 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only".

example.title: Understanding the Periodic Extension of a Function

question.text: \[ \langle f(x),g(x) \rangle = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2\pi} f(x) g(x) \, \textrm{d}x \] Given the inner product on the set of continuous functions over $x\in [0,2\pi)$ defined above, select the correct options below.
question.explanation:
We begin by using the product-to-sum identity \[ \sin(3x)\cos(4x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\sin(7x)-\sin(x)\big). \]

Substituting this into the integral gives \begin{align*} \langle \sin(3x), \cos(4x) \rangle &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \sin(3x)\cos(4x)\,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{2\pi} \dfrac{1}{2}\sin(7x)-\dfrac{1}{2}\sin(x) \:\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ -\dfrac{1}{14}\cos(7x)+\dfrac{1}{2}\cos(x) \right]_{0}^{2\pi} \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{14}\big(\cos(14\pi)-\cos(0)\big)+\dfrac{1}{2}\big(\cos(2\pi)-\cos(0)\big) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{14}(1-1)+\dfrac{1}{2}(1-1) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{0}. \end{align*}

Therefore, $f(x)=\sin(3x)$ and $g(x)=\cos(4x)$ $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{are orthogonal}}$ with respect to the inner product.
